title: Cheese Pizza, School Lunch, Thin Crust

content.title: About
content.content: Thin‑crust cheese pizza served in school cafeterias is a dish made from leavened wheat dough topped with tomato sauce and melted cheese. The dough is prepared with flour, water, yeast and a pinch of salt, and after baking it becomes crisp and light. The pizza provides carbohydrates, protein and calcium as part of a balanced school meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin crust allows faster baking in large batches, which is ideal for school kitchens.
The cheese used is often a blend of mozzarella and processed cheese to keep costs low.
Serving pizza in schools became popular in the 1990s as part of nutrition diversification programs.
School pizza sauce is usually made without added sugar to reduce calorie content.
A thin crust contains fewer calories than a traditional thick crust, making it more suitable for children’s diets.

items.title: Calcium source
items.content: Cheese supplies a substantial amount of calcium, essential for bone growth in children.

items.title: Good protein content
items.content: Both the dough and cheese provide a mix of plant‑based and dairy proteins that support tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tomatoes and yeast‑leavened dough contain vitamins B1, B2 and B6, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Lycopene in tomato sauce
items.content: Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, an antioxidant that may protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Lower fat level
items.content: The thin crust and moderate cheese amount make this pizza less fatty than traditional versions.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Children with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein allergy may react to the cheese.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheese and sauce can contain added salt, so sodium intake should be monitored.

items.title: Gluten in the dough
items.content: Standard wheat dough contains gluten, which is a concern for children with celiac disease.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Even with a thin crust, a serving can be calorie‑dense if eaten in large portions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut the pizza into bite‑size slices and serve warm. Adding fresh vegetables such as tomatoes or cucumber, or a sprinkle of herbs, can boost nutritional value. A light dusting of oregano is optional.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in an oven or microwave to keep the crust crisp.
